Beyond Fixed Chunks: How Semantic Chunking and Metadata Enrichment Transform RAG Accuracy
The difference between a RAG system that “kind of works” and one that delivers precise answers lies in how you chunk your data.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become the default architecture for building AI systems that answer questions over private data - documents, knowledge bases, reports, emails, and more.
The concept is simple: chunk your documents, embed them, store them in a vector database, and retrieve relevant pieces when a user asks a question. Feed those pieces to an LLM, and you get grounded, contextual answers.
But here’s the problem most teams discover after their first deployment:
The answers are mediocre. Not wrong enough to be obvious, but not right enough to be trusted.
The root cause, more often than not, is how the data was chunked.
This article explores why traditional fixed-size chunking fails at scale, and how two techniques - semantic chunking and LLM-powered metadata enrichment - can dramatically improve both retrieval precision and answer quality.
The Traditional RAG Pipeline - And Where It Breaks
The standard RAG pipeline looks like this:
1.
Ingest documents (PDFs, text, HTML, etc.)
2.
Chunk them into fixed-size pieces (e.g., 500 tokens with 50-token overlap)
3.
Embed each chunk into a vector
4.
Store vectors in a vector database
5.
Retrieve top-K similar chunks for a user query
6.
Generate an answer using the retrieved chunks as context
Why Fixed-Size Chunking Fails
Fixed-size chunking treats documents like a string of characters to be sliced at regular intervals. It has no understanding of what the text actually says. This creates several problems:
1. Semantic Boundaries Get Destroyed
A paragraph explaining revenue growth might be split across two chunks. The first chunk has the numbers, the second has the context. Neither chunk alone answers the question properly.
2. Tables and Structured Data Break Apart
Financial statements, factsheets, and reports are full of tables. Fixed chunking slices through table rows, separating headers from values and making the data meaningless.
3. Retrieval Returns “Sort-of Related” Results
When chunks carry incomplete ideas, embeddings become fuzzy. The vector search returns chunks that are adjacent to the answer rather than chunks that contain the answer.
4. No Filtering Capability
Need all chunks from Q3 2025? Or only from the risk factors section? Fixed chunking stores flat text with no structured metadata - every query hits the entire corpus with pure vector similarity.
5. Overlap Creates Redundancy
The standard fix - overlapping chunks - means the same sentences appear in multiple chunks, inflating storage and confusing retrieval with near-duplicate results.
Semantic Chunking - Letting Meaning Define Boundaries
Instead of splitting at arbitrary token counts, semantic chunking splits where the meaning shifts. The result: each chunk carries a complete, coherent idea.
There are two primary approaches:
Approach 1: Embedding-Based Semantic Chunking
This method uses embedding similarity to detect topic transitions:
1.
Segment the document into individual sentences
2.
Embed each sentence using an embedding model
3.
Compare consecutive sentence embeddings for similarity
4.
Split where similarity drops below a threshold - indicating a topic shift
When similarity between sentence N and sentence N+1 drops sharply, that’s a natural boundary. The sentences before and after that point belong to different topics.
Threshold methods:
•
Percentile - split when similarity drops below the 95th percentile of all differences
•
Standard deviation - split when the drop exceeds 3 standard deviations from the mean
•
Interquartile range - uses the middle 50% of scores to identify outliers
The result is variable-size chunks - some might be 200 tokens, others 1,500 - but each one represents a coherent unit of information.
Approach 2: LLM-Based Chunking
For higher accuracy (at higher cost), use an LLM to analyze document structure and decide where to split:
1.
Send the document (or large sections) to an LLM
2.
Instruct it to identify logical section breaks based on content, topic shifts, and argument flow
3.
Receive split points with section titles and classifications
4.
Create chunks using the LLM’s suggested boundaries
The LLM understands context far better than embedding similarity. It can recognize that a paragraph is a conclusion to the previous section (not the start of a new one), or that a table and its preceding description should stay together.
Advanced variant - Agentic Chunking:
An even more sophisticated approach converts sentences into standalone propositions first:
•
Original: “He led the Q3 review and noted a 12% increase.”
•
Proposition: “The CFO led the Q3 2025 earnings review and noted a 12% year-over-year revenue increase.”
Then an LLM evaluates each proposition: “Does this belong with the current chunk, or should I start a new one?” This produces chunks where every sentence makes sense independently - dramatically improving retrieval quality.
Why Semantic Chunking Improves Accuracy
Research shows semantic chunking can improve recall by up to 9% over simpler methods - and in domains like finance and legal, that gap often means the difference between a useful answer and a hallucinated one.
Metadata Enrichment - The Secret Weapon for Precision Retrieval
Semantic chunking solves the boundary problem. But there’s a second, equally important problem: finding the right chunks in the first place.
Vector similarity search alone has a fundamental limitation - it can only match on semantic meaning. It cannot filter by date, document type, topic category, or any structured attribute.
This is where LLM-powered metadata enrichment transforms RAG systems.
The Concept
After semantically chunking your documents, pass each chunk through an LLM to generate structured metadata:
•
Topic / Category - “Revenue Analysis”, “Risk Factors”, “Fund Performance”
•
Time Period - “Q3 2025”, “FY2024”, “January 2025”
•
Entities - company names, fund names, people, tickers
•
Metrics - AUM, NAV, returns, ratios, percentages
•
Document Type - factsheet, annual report, research note, earnings call transcript
•
Section Type - executive summary, methodology, conclusion, appendix
•
Sentiment / Outlook - positive, negative, neutral, cautious
These metadata fields are stored alongside the vector embedding in your database - as filterable, queryable fields.
How Metadata Generation Works in Practice
For a financial factsheet chunk, the LLM might generate:
{ "chunk_text": "The fund delivered a return of 14.2% in Q3 2025, outperforming the benchmark by 1.8%. AUM grew to $3.2B...", "metadata": { "topic": "Fund Performance", "time_period": "Q3 2025", "entities": ["Apex Global Growth Fund"], "metrics": { "return": "14.2%", "benchmark_alpha": "1.8%", "aum": "$3.2B" }, "document_type": "factsheet", "section_type": "performance_summary" }, "embedding": [0.023, -0.041, 0.087, ...] }
For different data types, the metadata schema adapts:
Why Metadata Matters - The Factsheet Example
Factsheets are a perfect illustration of why metadata is critical. They share several characteristics with other recurring, metrics-heavy documents:
•
Same structure, different data - every monthly factsheet has the same sections but updated numbers
•
Time-sensitive - last month’s returns are useless if you need this month’s
•
Metric-dense - users query by specific numbers, not vague topics
•
High volume - dozens of funds × monthly updates = thousands of documents
Without metadata, asking “What was the AUM of Fund X in September 2025?” forces a pure vector search across every factsheet ever stored. The retrieval might return chunks from March 2024 that happen to mention similar numbers.
With metadata, the query becomes:
1.
Filter: fund_name = "Fund X" AND time_period = "September 2025"
2.
Search: vector similarity within the filtered subset
3.
Result: the exact chunk with September 2025 AUM data
Other document types that benefit from the same pattern:
•
Fund NAV updates - filter by fund + date, search for specific metrics
•
Earnings call transcripts - filter by company + quarter, search for guidance or specific topics
•
Regulatory filings - filter by filing type + date, search for specific provisions
•
Credit rating reports - filter by issuer + agency, search for outlook changes
•
Economic reports - filter by region + period, search for specific indicators
Metadata-Powered Retrieval - From Fuzzy to Precise
With semantic chunks and enriched metadata in place, retrieval transforms from a single-axis similarity search into a multi-dimensional, filtered search.
How It Works
Traditional Retrieval:
User Query → Embed → Vector Search (entire corpus) → Top-K chunks → LLM
Problem: No way to constrain the search. Returns chunks from wrong time periods, wrong documents, wrong topics.
Metadata-Powered Retrieval:
User Query → Extract Filters (LLM/rules) → Metadata Pre-Filter → Vector Search (filtered subset) → Top-K chunks → LLM
The query itself can be analyzed to extract filter intent:
•
“What was the Global Growth Fund’s return last quarter?” → filter: fund_name="Apex Global Growth", time_period="Q3 2025"
•
“Compare risk factors across 2024 annual reports” → filter: document_type="annual_report", time_period="2024", topic="Risk Factors"
•
“Latest credit rating changes for XYZ Corp” → filter: entity="XYZ Corp", sort by date descending
The Impact
Advanced Techniques Worth Knowing
Beyond semantic chunking and metadata, several other techniques can further improve RAG accuracy:
1. Hierarchical / Parent-Child Chunking
Create two levels of chunks:
•
Parent chunks (1,000–2,000 tokens) - preserve broad context
•
Child chunks (200–500 tokens) - enable precise matching
Index child chunks for retrieval, but return parent chunks to the LLM. This gives you precise matching and full context - the best of both worlds.
Example: A user asks about “connection timeout settings.” The child chunk about timeout configuration matches precisely. But the LLM receives the entire “Database Configuration” parent section, including prerequisites and related parameters.
2. Late Chunking
Standard approach: chunk first, embed later. Late chunking: embed first, chunk later.
Process the entire document through a long-context embedding model first. Every token gets embedded with full document context. Then split into chunks - each chunk’s embeddings carry semantic information from the whole document.
This solves the pronoun and cross-reference problem: “The system” in chunk 47 still knows which system was introduced in chunk 2.
Best for: Technical documentation, academic papers, and any content with heavy cross-referencing.
3. Contextual Chunking
Before storing each chunk, prepend a brief summary of the full document:
[Document: Apex Global Growth Fund Factsheet, September 2025] [Section: Performance Summary]
The fund delivered a return of 14.2% in Q3 2025...
This gives every chunk document-level context without requiring the retrieval system to fetch additional metadata at query time.
4. Hybrid Routing by Document Type
Different documents need different strategies:
Build a document classifier at the front of your pipeline that routes each document to the appropriate chunking strategy.
The RAG Accuracy Improvement Pyramid
Think of RAG accuracy improvements as layers, each building on the previous:
You don’t need every technique. But moving from Level 0 to Level 2 - semantic chunking with metadata enrichment - delivers the highest ROI for most enterprise use cases.
Conclusion
The era of “just chunk it into 500 tokens and throw it in a vector DB” is over.
Modern RAG systems demand:
1.
Semantic chunking - let meaning, not character count, define chunk boundaries
2.
Metadata enrichment - use LLMs to generate structured, filterable metadata for every chunk
3.
Hybrid retrieval - combine metadata pre-filtering with vector similarity for precise, fast results
4.
Strategy per document type - route different documents through appropriate chunking pipelines
For teams working with factsheets, financial reports, research notes, and other recurring, metrics-heavy documents, metadata enrichment isn’t optional - it’s the difference between a RAG system that guesses and one that knows.
The investment in smarter chunking and metadata pays for itself quickly: fewer hallucinations, faster retrieval, better user trust, and a system that actually scales.
Start with semantic chunking. Add metadata. Watch your accuracy transform.
